EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

PO/BA harness: from business need to PRD

The PO/BA harness helps product owners (POs) and business analysts (BAs) turn a business need into a product requirements document (PRD): business-level user stories, acceptance criteria and, where useful, an HTML prototype. Choose one of three paths, then commit the artefacts and hand them to the development team.

The harness does not govern how you gather requirements. The three paths are starting points that suit different levels of technical experience and feature complexity. For the strategy behind the handoff, including what makes a PRD ready, read the handover section in Product ideation.

Choose a path

Pick the path that matches who is writing the requirements and how much is still unknown. Each path produces a different set of files, but all three end in the same handoff.

Path 1 suits simple or well-defined features and produces a spec.md file. Path 2 suits large or ambiguous features and produces an early-draft TRD on the issue tracker. Path 3 suits user research on new products and produces specification files in a specs/ folder. Each path can add a prototype, and each ends with the same commit and handoff.

The three PO/BA paths compared
PathBest forMain toolsHands off
1. SpecKitNon-technical POs or BAs with simple or well-defined featuresSpecKit, with optional Google Stitch, Figma Make or an agent-built HTML prototypespec.md and an optional prototype
2. Socratic workflowTechnical POs or BAs with large, ambiguous features whose scope is unclear/wayfinder, /grilling, /prototype, /to-specAn early-draft TRD on the tracker and an optional prototype branch
3. CLARA researchPOs or BAs researching users for a new product or complex featureCLARA, querying Confluence, with Prizm Design components for prototypesSpecification files in specs/ and an optional prototype

Source: [1] section 1.

Path 1: SpecKit, for simple or well-defined features

Use this path when the feature is understood and you need clear user stories quickly. SpecKit is GitHub’s open-source toolkit for spec-driven development; follow its own guide for the full command set.

  1. Generate the specification. Run /speckit.constitution, then /speckit.specify. The output is a spec.md file with the functional requirements and core user stories.
  2. Optionally, design or prototype the interface. Validate the requirements visually with stakeholders using one of three approaches:
    • Manual: paste the user stories into Google Stitch or Figma Make to generate a design or functional prototype.
    • Agentic: run stitch::generate-design from the Stitch skills inside your coding agent, passing the user stories as input.
    • Agent-built HTML: ask your coding agent to generate a standalone HTML prototype from the user stories.
  3. Optionally, hand off the prototype. Commit it alongside spec.md so developers can extract reusable UI components and keep screens consistent. For a Google Stitch project, developers run stitch::react-components or stitch::shadcn-ui. For a standalone HTML file, they use /html-to-shadcn Planned.

Source: [1] section 1, Path 1.

Path 2: Socratic workflow, for large or ambiguous features

Use this path when the full scope is unclear and requirements cannot be written until open questions are answered. It uses Matt Pocock’s skills to map the unknowns, resolve them one at a time and record the decisions.

  1. Map the unknowns. Run /wayfinder. It creates a shared map of investigation tickets on the issue tracker and labels each by the type of work it needs.
  2. Resolve the tickets one at a time, using the skill that matches each label (see the table below).
  3. Write the specification. Run /to-spec to compile the decisions, codebase constraints and prototype outcomes into an early-draft technical requirements document (TRD). It is published to the issue tracker as the handoff artefact.
  4. Optionally, hand off a UI prototype. If a prototype ticket produced UI variations, retrieve them from the prototype/<name> branch and hand them off with the specification. Developers can then use /html-to-shadcn Planned to extract reusable components.
Wayfinder ticket labels and how each is resolved
LabelHow it is resolved
wayfinder:grilling/grilling interviews the PO or BA until there is a shared understanding, building the domain model and updating architecture decision records (ADRs) as it goes.
wayfinder:prototype/prototype builds a throwaway prototype to answer a design question: one shareable HTML file to test a logic or state model, or several HTML UI variations to settle what a screen should look like.
wayfinder:researchA background research agent explores third-party APIs, documentation or codebase constraints.
wayfinder:taskManual setup work, such as provisioning access or migrating data, that unblocks a decision.

Source: [1] section 1, Path 2.

Path 3: product research with CLARA

Use this path when the team needs to understand users before it can detail functional requirements, such as for a new product or a complex feature. CLARA is an interactive research harness that queries Confluence to refine product concepts.

  1. Research and discover. Follow CLARA’s step-by-step research harness to gather and refine what is already known.
  2. Work through the design-thinking stages. Build user personas and journey maps, define the root-cause problem statement, generate solution ideas and converge on the best user experience.
  3. Write the specification. Generate the research artefacts and consolidated specification files, such as product-specifications.md or specs.md with the user stories, in a specs/ folder.
  4. Optionally, prototype the interface. Generate an HTML prototype of the chosen experience using Prizm Design components, and hand it off with the specification files as a visual reference.

CLARA can only ground its research in what it can reach. Make sure the team’s domain documentation is in the Confluence spaces or knowledge bases CLARA queries; read how to add domain context.

Sources: [1] section 1, Path 3; [2] section 1.

Commit the artefacts and hand off

Whichever path you choose, finish by committing the specification artefacts where the architect and developers can reach them. Then hand them over to start technical planning and sequencing.

What each path commits
PathSpecificationPrototype, if produced
1. SpecKitspec.md in the repositoryCommitted alongside the specification
2. Socratic workflowEarly-draft TRD published to the issue trackerReferenced through its prototype/<name> branch
3. CLARA researchSpecification files in specs/Committed alongside the specification files

Together, these files are the PRD: what needs to be built, captured as user stories, acceptance criteria and feature scope. The developer team sequences its user stories with /dependency-orchestrator and then writes a user story level TRD for each one. If you followed Path 2, /to-spec in the developer harness refines your early-draft TRD rather than starting from scratch.

Ground each path in your team’s vocabulary. Supply domain context, glossaries and functional requirements when you run /speckit.specify; reference domain models and legacy patterns when you run /wayfinder, with /domain-modeling and /codebase-design to keep the language consistent.

Next step: agree with your architect or Tech Lead where the PRD will live, then see how developers plan from it. If you are unsure which path fits, run /ask-workflow.

Sources: [1] section 1 and “From PO/BA handoff to developer”; [2] section 1.
